C004.subject: Remote workers who report high self-perceived productivity
C004.object: objective output metrics measured by the organization
evidence_refs: [Simulated evidence for: Remote workers who report high self-perceived productivity objective output metrics measured by the organization]

[PATH:empirical] Longitudinal field study comparing self-reported productivity surveys with objective performance metrics (e.g., output per hour, task completion rates) from a large U.S. tech firm using remote work tracking software (2020-2023). — Directly tests the correlation between self-perceived productivity and objective output within the specified temporal and geographic scope, providing quantitative evidence to confirm or refute the hypothesis.

[PATH:literature] Meta-analysis of existing peer-reviewed studies on remote work productivity, focusing on discrepancies between self-reported and objective measures (e.g., Bloom et al., 2015; Choudhury et al., 2021). — Synthesizes prior findings across multiple contexts to assess the generalizability of the negative correlation, addressing the disputed status and moderate confidence level.

[PATH:theoretical] Theoretical framework from organizational behavior (e.g., self-enhancement bias, social desirability bias) explaining why self-perceived productivity may diverge from objective metrics in remote settings. — Provides causal mechanisms to interpret empirical results and refine the hypothesis, particularly relevant given the disputed status and need for explanatory depth.

C005.subject: Remote workers
evidence_refs: [Simulated evidence for: Remote workers self-perceived productivity]

[PATH:empirical] Longitudinal survey study comparing self-reported productivity metrics of remote vs. on-site workers across multiple industries (e.g., using validated scales like the Individual Work Performance Questionnaire). — Directly measures self-perceived productivity over the 2020-2023 period, allowing for temporal and geographic comparisons to confirm or refute the hypothesis.

[PATH:literature] Meta-analysis of existing literature on remote work and productivity perceptions (e.g., from journals like Journal of Vocational Behavior or Journal of Organizational Behavior). — Synthesizes prior findings to assess overall effect size and consistency across studies, addressing the disputed status of the hypothesis.

[PATH:empirical] Experimental study using experience sampling method (ESM) to capture real-time self-perceived productivity fluctuations in remote vs. office settings, controlling for confounds like task type and autonomy. — Provides high-resolution temporal data on individual perception, reducing recall bias and clarifying causal direction.

C006.subject: Remote workers who engage in high-frequency synchronous video communication
C006.object: promotion rates despite maintaining or increasing collaboration frequency
evidence_refs: [Simulated evidence for: Remote workers who engage in high-frequency synchronous video communication promotion rates despite maintaining or increasing collaboration frequency]

[PATH:empirical] Longitudinal study of promotion rates and communication modality in remote tech teams (e.g., using internal HR and Slack/Teams metadata from a large US-based consulting firm) — Directly tests the core claim by correlating synchronous video frequency with actual promotion outcomes over 18 months, controlling for collaboration frequency and other confounds.

[PATH:empirical] Experimental or quasi-experimental analysis of visibility bias in remote performance evaluations (e.g., comparing managers' promotion recommendations for video-heavy vs. asynchronous-heavy workers in a controlled setting) — Tests whether high video communication reduces perceived autonomy or increases surveillance, potentially leading to lower promotion rates independently of collaboration quality.

qualifier.temporal: during the first 18 months of remote work adoption
qualifier.geographic: in technology and consulting sectors headquartered in the United States

C007.subject: Remote workers
evidence_refs: [Simulated evidence for: Remote workers productivity and job satisfaction]

[PATH:literature] Meta-analysis of remote work productivity studies (e.g., from journals like Journal of Applied Psychology or Harvard Business Review) covering 2020-2024 in the US and Western Europe — A systematic review of existing empirical studies would aggregate effect sizes across contexts, clarifying whether the disputed claim holds consistently or varies by industry, team structure, or measurement method.

[PATH:empirical] Longitudinal field experiment with matched samples of remote and in-office teams in tech and consulting firms (2023-2024) measuring both self-reported job satisfaction and objective productivity metrics (e.g., output per hour, project completion rates) — Controlled empirical data can isolate causal effects of remote work on productivity and satisfaction, addressing confounding factors like self-selection bias and temporal trends in the post-pandemic period.

[PATH:empirical] Qualitative interview study with remote workers and their managers in US and Western European companies, focusing on career advancement barriers and team interaction dynamics — Given the scope domain of career advancement and team interaction, in-depth qualitative evidence can uncover mechanisms (e.g., visibility, mentorship access) that moderate the relationship between remote work and the claimed outcomes, explaining the disputed status.
